title: Eighty thousand woodblocks
hook: after invaders burn the first set, Korea carves the whole canon again in wood: the Tripitaka Koreana

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chinul's frozen pond. See it's water at once, then let it thaw. Your line: sudden, then slowly.

A carver bends over a block of wood. On it, written backward so it will print the right way round, are the characters of a Buddhist scripture. He cuts away everything that isn't a letter. One slip of the knife and a word is gone. Around him, more blocks wait, and more after those, enough to fill a library. This is Korea under the Goryeo kings, and the reason for all this patient cutting is a fire.
screen: `A CARVER, A KNIFE, A BLOCK.` → `LETTERS CUT BACKWARD.` → `THE REASON IS A FIRE.`

segments.voice: Goryeo had already carved the Buddhist canon once, the Tripitaka, the three baskets of teaching. Then Mongol armies invaded, and that first set of blocks was burned. The court and the monks decided to carve the whole canon again. A prayer written for the work by the scholar Yi Gyubo asks the Buddhas and protectors to look on the effort and turn the invaders back. So the carving was scholarship and devotion at once: every block a page of scripture, and the whole a vow. The texts were compared and corrected against other editions before the cutting began. Tradition says the carvers bowed after each character. In Korea the collection is known as the Palman Daejanggyeong, the Eighty Thousand Tripitaka, after its blocks. Today they are kept at Haeinsa, a temple in the mountains, in long wooden halls built with slatted windows to let the air move through. A burned set taught them that words can be lost. Their answer wasn't despair, and it wasn't speed. It was slowness, done right. Some things are made to be used up today. Others are made to outlast the people who made them. The carvers of Goryeo chose the second kind, one letter at a time.
screen: `THE FIRST SET BURNED.` · `CARVED AGAIN AS A VOW.` · `A BOW, TRADITION SAYS, FOR EACH CHARACTER.` · `KEPT AT HAEINSA.` · then, large: `CARVED TO LAST.`

segments.voice: If you have paper and a pen, take them; if not, trace with a finger on your palm. Write one line that matters to you, a name or a sentence you want to keep, as slowly as you can, one letter at a time, as if it had to last a long time.
Tripitaka Koreana. The Buddhist canon carved again in wood after invaders burned the first set, and kept at Haeinsa.
Your line: carved to last. Slowness, done right, outlasted the fire. Day nine hundred twenty-three, done.

chat.says: Why would anyone carve a whole library of scripture in wood twice?
options: A Mongol invasion burned the first set, so they carved it all again, as a vow.
The first set was full of errors, so the king had it all thrown out.
Paper was forbidden in Korea then, so wood was the only way to write.
chat.meaning: Mongol armies burned Goryeo's first set of blocks. Court and monks carved the canon again, checked and corrected, as scholarship and a vow.
